speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TERMINATION OF ACTIVITIES IN OBTAINING FUNDS FOR PROSECUTION OF THE WAR
speechtext:
I wish to announce to the house that the national war finance committee has recommended the termination of its active life. I have accepted this recommendation. It is not possible at this time to decide the nature of further campaigns for the sale of government securities which may be required in the future. It is therefore appropriate that the great organization set up to obtain funds for the successful prosecution of the war should end its career on the conclusion of its greatest achievement, the ninth victory loan. The final figures for this loan will be in excess of two billion dollars, of which amount approximately $1,200 million represents investments by individuals.
It is not my intention to outline the accomplishments of the national war finance committee in detail, but I think it is fitting that the house should take note of the end of this organization and that the record should show the names of the major organizations which contributed to its work.
As members are doubtless aware, much of the executive personnel of the national war finance committee was drawn from the ranks of the investment dealers of Canada. They

have supplied in large measure the working machinery for the operation. Other groups in the Canadian financial world have made substantial contributions. Among them, the chartered banks of Canada assumed a large burden in connection with the sale and delivery of bonds. The Life Officers Association and the Life Underwriters of Canada have also facilitated the building of a sales organization. Leaders in agricultural and labour organizations have provided advice and assistance. Among these groups appear the names of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Canadian Congress of Labour, Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the Canadian and Catholic Federation of Labour and the General Conference Committee of the Standard Railway Labour Organizations.
In the sales structure evolved by the national war finance committee certain special war organizations were required to meet special circumstances. The victory loan committees of the armed forces are a case in point. The results achieved by this group were a substantial element of the total' sales reported from individuals. Further, the armed forces provided important aid to public events to stimulate general public interest. Mention should also be made of the accomplishments of the civil service in organizing and promoting their internal canvasses.
Finally, the sales organization of the national war finance committee was greatly benefited by the leadership of business executives in facilitating the canvass of their employees, and in stimulating public response. The executive personnel of the Canadian Pacific Railways and the Canadian National Railways provide examples of this typ^ of leadership, which was repeated thousands of times across the country.
Although I have mentioned some of the organizations assisting in the sales operations, the accomplishments of the national war finance committee would not have been possible without the help of the Canadian publishers war finance publicity committee, a joint organization representing all publishers of Canada which has given invaluable advice and recommendations with reference to publicity. Associated with this committee, the advertising agencies of Canada have rendered expert service. The national radio committee, representing the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the advertising agencies of Canada, has performed a similar function in the field of broadcasting. The war services committee of the Canadian motion picture industry and its affiliated organizations in the United States

War Finance Committee
provided essential assistance in their field, both in the production and distribution of special films, and in the placing of their establishments at the disposal of the national war finance committee for public gatherings. The national film board was of major assistance in the production of special films and in respect to distribution of films, particularly in the 16-millimetre circuits. We are also indebted to the Outdoor Advertising Association and to the Canadian Street-car Advertising Company which gave their support in generous measure.
These and many other institutions and individuals gave powerful impetus to the work of the national war finance committee. I shall not attempt to name them all at this time because of the urgent affairs which claim the attention of the house. I believe, however, that the members will agree that the main credit for its success should go to the thousands of loyal workers throughout the country who have constituted plant victory loan committees or who served as chairmen of units and subunits, and in countless other assignments necessary to the success of our war financing programme. They have rendered a great service to their country. And finally I should say that the work of all these people would have been of little avail if the Canadian public had not been willing and anxious to assume their full financial responsibility for the winning of the war.
Suggestions have come to me from many quarters that suitable facilities be provided by the government for a continuing savings programme to commence next autumn when final instalments in the ninth victory loan have been paid. I should like to advise the house that t-his matter is being given careful study. In the meantime, war savings stamps and war savings certificates will continue to be available through normal channels, probably until the fall of 1946.
I do not wish to conclude without reference to the effective efforts of hundreds of voluntary workers, many of them women, on behalf of the sale of war savings stamps and certificates. The gross sales of war savings certificates before redemption since May 1940, and the unredeemed stamps still in the hands of the public, amount to the combined total of approximately $365,000,000, a substantial sum indeed to obtain from small savings over this period. School teachers have inspired thousands of school children to invest savings ! which are included in this total. War savings stamps are still being purchased steadily
through the operation of the current school savings plan. It is my intention to ask each province for their views on a continuance of this plan as a means of teaching regular savings habits to students. If they so desire, it will be continued in a form suited to the new circumstances.
But my main purpose to-day is served by announcing the cessation of the national war finance committee. I know all members of this house will join me in expressing deep appreciation of its work. It has been an important faptor in the winning of the war and in anchoring the economy against the shock of war. The results may well be an even more important influence for the future well-being of the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TERMINATION OF ACTIVITIES IN OBTAINING FUNDS FOR PROSECUTION OF THE WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad
to add my word of commendation to that already extended by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to the national war finance committee which the minister has announced is being discontinued. I am sure we all feel that that organization has performed an outstanding service to Canada during the last half dozen years. We are all agreed that all those associated with it, from the Minister of Finance and the chairman of the committee down, including the officials and the workers in whatever capacity, deserve the unstinted praise and thanks of this house and of the Canadian people.

maintopic: TERMINATION OF ACTIVITIES IN OBTAINING FUNDS FOR PROSECUTION OF THE WAR
speechtext: I think we can all agree with what the leader of the opposition has said. Our' thanks go out not only to those who organized the campaign, but also to the hundreds and thousands. ves, millions of Canadians who supported the campaign so overwhelmingly. I am particularly glad to note that the minister referred to the teachers in the schools. He suggests that inquiry is to be made of the departments of education with regard to the continuation of something of this kind. While the teachers willingly gave support to the war-time loans, I doubt whether it is proper and fair to ask them to continue this activity into the peace years, having regard to the burdens that they are carrying in the schools at the present time.

These estimates were last before the committee prior to the conference held in Ottawa with regard to agricultural production for the coming year. That conference is over now and I believe certain decisions were reached with respect to production. Can the minister tell us what those decisions were? I should like particularly to have something said in regard to the production of wheat, as to whether under present world conditions we are to continue our production at the same rate or whether that production is to be increased. It was reported also to have been suggested to the various organizations represented at that conference that we should have an increase in the production of pork during the coming year, and I should like to ask the minister what steps the department is taking to bring about that increased production. It does not seem to me they are likely to get it unless some definite steps are taken toward that end. During the war years we demonstrated just what could be done with respect to increasing agricultural production in any particular branch if the government were prepared to make price concessions, and I have doubt whether we shall get any increase in the production of pork unless some change is made in government policy. I think the minister should give us a statement as to the conclusions reached at this conference.

Egg production in Canada for 1945 is now estimated at 395 million dozen, the highest figure in the country's history, and exceeding the previous year by 34 million dozen. Quantities purchased by the special products board in fulfilment of the British contract totalled 90 million dozen, exceeding 1944 by 10 million dozen. Domestic use, estimated at 291 million dozen, was heavier than the 1940-44 average by 37 million dozen.
Production estimates for 1946 are based on chick hatches and sales in the 1945 season. There is now a carry-over of matured stock and anticipated early hatchings in 1946 from which fall eggs in 1946 will be produced. It is estimated that 1946 production will be 17 million dozen less than in 1945 and 18 million dozen more than in 1944. Hatches in 1945 based on approved hatchery figures were fourteen per cent under 1944. All provinces showed a decrease with the exception of Prince Edward Island, which recorded an eight per cent increase. An increase is anticipated for 1946, particularly in early hatches.
Eggs available for export in 1946, after allowing for a continued heavy domestic use, due to meat rationing, are estimated at 88 million dozen. The quantity will be approximately sufficient to fill the 1946 contract with the British ministry of food. I am glad that the minister is getting closer and closer to those of us who sit in this corner, and I hope he continues this policy. The dominion and provincial governments are to be commended for the discussions which have been carried on recently. I hope they will realize their ambition. but mother nature may have something to say about all their plans. It does not make any difference how ambitious your plans are on paper, one night of frost or fifteen minutes of hail will destroy all your good intentions.
In order to aid nature in carrying out this programme something should be done in the way of increasing prices of the different farm commodities. The minister has told us on many occasions that at the present time we are receiving above parity prices for many of our farm products, but I should like to remind him that the period taken as a base for parity is 1926-29 when the farmers were receiving only 16-6 per cent of the national income. That is not a good enough percentage of the national income upon which to figure parity prices. If we took the prices that existed in 1915-19 as a parity base the farmers of Canada would get to work and do something worthwhile in the production of live stock, grain and other farm products. Until that is done I do not think the government can expect the farmers to get right down to business and produce as they should produce during the coming j^ear.
Take wheat for example. When the export price reached $1.55 a bushel, a ceiling rvas placed on the price, temporarily at least. By that method the farmers were expected to make enormous gifts to other countries which

are using our wheat. Those gifts should be made by the people of Canada as a whole. The farmers of Canada should be paid the full present price. I realize that we have a floor under the price which will prevent it from dropping below $1 per bushel basis Fort William until after the end of August, 1950. But that is not good enough, because deliveries will be restricted and many of us will not be able to take advantage of the $1 per bushel basis Fort William. The government will have to revise radically its programme and do something to put the price up to where it properly belongs. We have been fooled in the past, at least some of us have, by being told that we were getting parity prices or above parity prices; I do not think that policy is going to carry out any longer. The production records show that the farmers are not doing their utmost and will not do their utmost until prices are radically raised.

To the best of my knowledge, the Minister of Agriculture has never made an official visit to my constituency of Kootenay West, and on behalf of the agricultural organizations of that riding I want to extend a hearty invitation to the minister to visit us. In the interior of British Columbia there has been in recent years a great expansion of poultry production and in the organization of poultry producers. Throughout the war there developed an unsatisfactory situation with regard to the egg inspection service. Far too many ungraded eggs are being sold in the interior of British Columbia, and the organized poultry producers consider this to be a most unfair
situation. They have not pressed the matter previously because they realized there was a shortage of staff due to the war, but I should like to ask the minister what he intends to do to correct this situation.
May I suggest to the hon. member that he leave this until we reach the item having to do with marketing. All the inspection services having to do with quality come under marketing.

In recent years the Department of Agriculture have subsidized the shipment of coarse grains and other grains to eastern Canada. This has been continued to the extent that it is no longer profitable for farmers in the west to raise hogs, and production has gone down at a terrific rate. What does it cost the Canadian government to ship this feed eastward? Does the Canadian government intend to continue the policy of having the Canadian taxpayer pay the cost of shipping this feed to eastern farmers when there are many farmers in the west who would like to use their feed in the raising of hogs?

The correction I want to make is this. There is no authority anywhere, east or west, who would say that it does not pay the farmer who produces the grain in western Canada to feed grain to hogs. Anybody feeding grain to hogs can make more money that way, and some claim to be able to make fifty per cent more, depending on the kind of hogs they have and on their facilities for feeding them. Most hog producers say that they can feed at a considerable profit. There is no authority anywhere, so far as departmental officials are concerned, and they are the real authorities, who would say that it does not pay to feed grain to hogs. We are feeding hogs at our experimental farms under test. The one place where we are feeding them consistently is on the farm in Alberta, and all the reports from there indicate that hogs can be produced to advantage even at the present prices of grain. I feed hogs myself; I would not do so if I did not think I could make more money feeding hogs than by selling the grain.
There is a fifty per cent reduction.
Because there is a fifty per cent reduction in feed grain. I cannot understand why those who discuss this question will not get down to the practical side.
Are you not shipping grain eastward?
Yes, and hogs are being fed in the east to as great an extent as in the years before the war.

In the section of the
country in which I live there has been no shortage of feed grain in the last four years; our production of grain has been just about the same. Nevertheless the farmers have reduced their hog production by thirty-five per cent. That is the real test, whether the farmer considers the price advantageous. If he does, he will continue to produce, but hog production has dropped in the area I represent. It is not a shortage of grain which has stopped hog production, because the grain is there to feed. The reason is that the farmers do not consider that there is a reasonable margin.

If my hon. friend and I at our age were asked to feed hogs we probably would not think solely of the profit we were going to make out of it, particularly if we had been making a little profit in the last five or six years and had got ourselves into fairly good circumstances as compared with other times. We would probably say: We are not going to feed hogs this winter but will take a little rest. A lot of farmers are saying that. It is not because they cannot get more for their hogs; they know they can. My hon. friend knows he can get more for the grain fed to hogs, if he feeds them properly, than he can get by selling the grain. Every practical farmer knows that. But many farmers are getting older and they feel they do not wrant to feed hogs. There are also those who are coming back to farming who were accustomed to producing grain before the war, and they want to continue to produce grain rather than feed live stock. Some of those are not going into the feeding of live stock.
We rather feel this way about it, that we can produce in this country only the number of hogs and cattle that we can feed with our own grain. Some countries import grain and feed live stock on imported grain, but our markets are too far away for that. We do not import grain for the purpose of feeding live stock. We know that we cannot feed the live stock that we have on our farms at, the present time on the average production of grain; everyone knows that, and you have to consider that, when you are considering the amount of live stock you are going to feed in

Canada. We feel that in the years ahead of us we are not going to market outside of Canada more hogs than we are marketing outside Canada now. We probably could for another year, maybe two years, market more outside Canada, but we certainly are not figuring that we shall be able to market more hogs outside Canada in the future than we are marketing now. In addition, we do feel that we shall market many more hogs in Canada than we are marketing at present, because we have been restricting the marketing of hogs in Canada all though the war in order to send the hogs to Britain to help them, and we have cut down the consumption of hogs in our own country. So it probably would not be right to say that we cannot market more hogs than we are producing at the present time. When you take the two markets together, the home and the foreign market, we may be able to market more hogs than we are now producing.
We feel that there are many farmers in Canada who want to produce hogs. There are many others who do not want to produce hogs. There is a greater percentage in eastern Canada than in Western Canada of farmers who either want to produce hogs or feel that they must produce hogs if they are to exist on their farms. - There are in western Canada areas like the Melfort district, of which the hon. member spoke, of which that is not true, but the Melfort district is the best hog-producing area in Saskatchewan, and one of the best in western Canada. So we are hopeful, and I think we have reason for expecting our hopes to be fulfilled, that the farmers in that area will still continue to produce hogs. When we pome to the drought area, where the drough is extreme, we can expect many of those who have been producing hogs under pressure in war time not to continue to produce hogs to as great an extent in the future.	i
So, as we go across Canada, we feel that we shall have to encourage some people to produce grain which they themselves are not going to feed, and to ship it to some other part of Canada where fanners either want to feed hogs or feel they must feed hogs because it pays them better. It is only by a proper distribution of the grain that we can produce the type of hog we want. We do not say to every farmer: We want you to feed all your grain. We say that on the whole we want a production of grain that will make possible the peak of hog production, and we want the grain distributed in such a way as to keep the man producing hogs who feels that he can produce at a profit and is producing the type of hog we want for the markets we have to

supply, more particularly the British market, where we are in competition with Danish producers.

Just before the minister leaves the question of hog production may I ask a question? Have not the income tax exemptions been one reason for the decreased hog production on the prairies? The Minister of Agriculture may not want to answer that question directly, but he knows that under the income tax law, married couples where the wife is working in a factory are allowed an exemption of $1,800. It is admitted that this is WTong in principle, but it was simply to increase war production. The people on the farms have been allowed only SI,200. I repeat what I said the other day, that the income tax collectors have done a real job of collecting in my province of Manitoba in the last three years. They have gone to the municipal offices and I have been there when farmers were there and I have heard farmers say. "When I go home I am not going to raise any hogs." Farmer after farmer has taken that attitude. Owing to the fact that he can make a fair living in the production of grain, he and his family are not likely to work long hours before daylight and hours after dark in an effort to produce hogs when they are exempt on $1,200, while their city friends have been exempted to the extent of $1,800. That has had more to do with the decline in hog production on the prairies than anything else, and I am sure the minister will agree with me in that regard.

That, I believe, is really part of the answer to the question raised by the member for Melfort. He asked me why it was that men in that district were going down in hog production, notwithstanding that they had grain with which to feed hogs in that area. I believe I have more letters in which it, is contended that the income tax is responsible than I have letters assigning the cause to any other factor. I think that is part and parcel of the situation. Anyone who has made out an income tax return knows that all the profit is not taken away from him. When a man says it is because he has to pay income tax on the hogs produced or on the butter he produces, that is not quite correct. You cannot say that you will put it all on wheat, because it. is easier to produce wheat than the

other commodities. After all, when you make up your income tax, you take your wheat, butter and everything else, put them in together and get the total income, so that only part of the profit and not all is taken.
I did not say it was all taken.

I am not saying that the hon. gentleman did. I am answering the suggestion made that the reason is the income tax. It is income tax to this extent. A man says to himself: I have been working hard at this and I have done fairly well. At the beginning of the war I was not in the income tax brackets at all and now I am and I have to pay income tax. There is no doubt that he gets probably only sixty per cent of the profit he would otherwise get, and that has something to do with his quitting the production of hogs. But the real reason is that he feels he is getting along fairly well without producing hogs; that much greater labour is involved in hog production than in producing grain; that he is now in the income tax brackets paying income tax; that he is living better than he did at one time; and in short that it is not worth the labour at his age to go in for hog production. In most cases that is why he says: "I am not going to work just to pay income tax." He puts it that way, but we all realize that the income tax does not take all his profits from him, because he still makes a profit on top of what he would otherwise make if he did not feed hogs.

The market at Calgary was $15.98; Edmonton, $15.92; Prince Albert, S16.03; Moose Jaw, $16.05; Saskatoon, $15.99; Regina, $16.03; Vancouver, $16.69 and Moncton down on the eastern coast, $17.22. In Toronto, for example, it varies from a high of $17.63 in December to a low of $17.11 in January of that year. The variation there is about fifty-two cents a hundred.
As I understand the question, it is why we have these variations at all. The question asked by the hon. member for The Battle-fords is as to why we had a drop in the fall of this year. I think the question he ought to ask me is, why did we have a rise in price? There has been no change whatsoever in the floor price created by the contract which we have had with Britain since the beginning of 1944. The average price in Toronto in 1944 was $17.25; in Winnipeg, $16.40, and that price or a little better price than that prevails at this moment. That is the price which is made possible by the sale of a certain proportion of the hogs under the

British contract, which is the floor price, and a certain proportion of the hogs on the Canadian market at the ceiling price. We have been discussing whether we should not have ceilings and floors. I see one hon. member smiling; because he is Irish he can smile at anything and change his mind. I imagine he thinks that is a ridiculous thing for a packer to do. I say this to him: in my experience with packers and every other person in business I find that the best of them take losses occasionally. They have to do that in order to keep their customers satisfied and in order that they may perhaps make a little more profit at some other time than they otherwise would get. During that particular period of time they did take losses occasionally. I have talked to most of them, and my information, for what it is worth, is that they all had losses during that period. A man who will not believe that of course will not accept what is the ordinary practice in connection with business of all kinds. People occasionally do take losses rather than be unable to supply their customers at all. As a matter of fact if there was somebody on the black market who had a sale for the product and was out bidding for it, so that another man was not going to be able to stock his shops with that product ' at a time when we were letting people in Canada eat all they liked of it, he would probably say, "Well, I have "to pay more and take a, loss in order to get hogs," and some of them may have done that. When we resumed rationing of meat in Canada the situation immediately began to adjust itself. We said we were going

I am interested in this item because unfortunately in the constituency which I represent we have had altogether too much Bang's disease. This is a cheese producing county, in fact it was due to the advertising received from a mammoth cheese constructed in Lanark county that we owe our present export trade in cheese to the British isles. It was back in 1893 that this large cheese was manufactured for publicity purposes. It wpighed eleven tons and was exhibited at the world's fair in Chicago. It crashed through the floor there and created more attention than ever. Later on it was exhibited in London, England, and it was through the publicity and advertising that it obtained that our export trade with that country was started.
The cheese producers and live stock breeders have had a lot of trouble because of Bang's disease. The exact time and manner in which cattle contract and spread Bang's disease or infect each other is not always an easy matter to establish. The disease is generally first introduced into a clean herd through unknowingly obtaining infected cattle from another herd. Once this happens the disease will go through a herd like a storm, and it may spread through a whole township or district. During the storm stage of the disease the highest losses are experienced. The usual experience is that during the first two or three years of the appearance of the disease many victims are claimed, but the casualties become reduced each year unless new stock is introduced or young stock are growing up, which in turn would become infected.
The cattle seem to develop a natural immunity, and the active losses are not so noticeable. When the disease does become acute the owner of the herd suffers severe losses in young stock, a drop in value occurs and he has difficulty in disposing of his herd. In order to determine whether animals are infected with this disease it is necessary to have them blood-tested and the specimen examined at a laboratory. If a large number of reactors are found it may be desirable to keep the herd intact, consider it an infected unit and deal with it under combined methods of sanitation, segregation and the inoculation of calves in an endeavour to build up a clean herd from the offspring.
The cost of this examination is paid for by the herd owner, that is, he must have the veterinary withdraw the blood and make the examination, although the laboratory people will do the work. In Ontario there are no provincial regulations regarding the sale of animals afflicted with Bang's disease, but it has been a common custom among pure-bred herd owners not to buy animals unless they

Supply-A griculture

are negative as to blood test. The best breeders strive to have negative herds, but in spite of all precautions the disease will find its way into the herd, with consequent financial loss to the owner.
The reason I am interested in this matter is that unfortunately the disease does not stop with the herd. Human beings may acquire the disease through handling infected cattle or using raw milk. In the human being it is called undulant fever. It is a rural disease, eighty per cent of the cases reported having occurred among farmers and their families. Butchers, truckers, veterinary surgeons and travellers account for the remainder of the cases through handling infected cattle or using raw milk. In Ontario, and I have studied this disease particularly in this province, the disease is highest in the counties of Middlesex, Waterloo, York, Oxford, Perth, Elgin, Simcoe, Essex, and is prevalent throughout eastern Ontario. During the past four years 321 cases of undulant fever have been reported in Ontario, with ten deaths. This is a reduction as compared with the years prior to the advent of pasteurization when 515 cases and twenty deaths were reported from 1934 to 1938. In connection with these statistics, which I obtained from the Ontario Department of Health, I would say of my own knowledge that for every case reported there probably would be five or six not reported. Sometimes the people affected with this disease are sick for months, and it may go on for years. They do not know what is the matter with them and many do not consult a doctor.
I have here some statistics showing the incidence of undulant fever in Ontario in the years 1934 to 1938, which I should like to place before the committee:	In 1934 the
Ontario Department of Health lists 97 cases of undulant fever, with three deaths, and a morbidity rate per 100,000 of 2-7 per cent; 1935, 86 cases, five deaths, morbidity rate 2-4 per cent; 1936, 127 cases, two deaths, morbidity rate 3-1 per cent; 1937, KM cases, seven deaths, morbidity rate 2-7 per cent; 1938, 101 cases, three deaths, 2 per cent.
Since pasteurization-and all the milk in Ontario is not pasteurized-there has been a marked drop since October 1, 1938, in the incidence of undulant fever, as is shown by the figures I have before me. This disease of undulant fever causes marked weakness and may run a course of two of three years. People afflicted with it suffer a most serious illness and during the more acute stages are confined to bed. They run a temperature for weeks and months, and the course of the disease is most debilitating. It is doubtful whether those who get it. ever regain normal health; the effects may show themselves in later years. There ia no doubt that a disease with such debilitating effects and lasting for such a long period takes a severe toll from the human body. There is no specific treatment for undulant fever; even penicillin has been tried with very little result. A medical man called in to treat a disease of that type can give only symptomatic treatment. He is helpless because we have nothing to stop the incidence of the disease. The table of statistics from the Ontario Department of Health shows that we are dealing with a disease that cannot be taken lightly. From 1940 to 1944 there were 321 cases reported, with ten deaths. If an accident occurred in any Canadian city, injuring 321 people and causing ten deaths, it would be headlined in the press throughout America as a tragedy.
In order to cure or get rid of undulant fever we have to go back and tackle Bang's disease. The control of this disease, with its tremendous loss to stock owners and the infection of

Supply-Agriculture
human beings with a morbidity rate of 1-6 per 100,000, I maintain is a problem for the federal Department of Health. It is clearly shown in the Animal Contagious Diseases Act that this is a responsibility of the federal Department of Agriculture. If this disease, which causes tremendous loss to stock owners and the infection of human beings to the extent I have mentioned continues to be dealt with in the manner in which it has been dealt with by the federal Department of Health, we shall have the disease rampant throughout the province.
I suggest that more money should be spent in the research branch of the Department of Agriculture to study the disease and to find methods of combating it. Dairy herd owners should receive assistance by free blood-testing of their herds under the supervision of the federal Department of Agriculture, and there should be more rigid control in segregating animals in infected districts. Other, measures such as the inoculation of young stock should also be free and carried out by the Department of Agriculture. Some financial compensation should be given to owners of the infected herds for losses sustained. This disease has been talked about for years and nothing done, so that we must approach it progressively. Clean herds should be kept clean; under the present situation they are not.
We believe the time has come when we ought to build up some protection against this disease by the vaccination of calves. We think the methods used in dealing with T.B. in cattle, whereby when seventy-five per cent of owners in a good area sign a petition asking the government to establish an area of segregation it becomes operative, should be followed in connection with this disease, and that all heifer calves in the area should be inoculated for immunization.
The objection to signing the form that is now required by the department, where all animals found to be, infectecT must be slaughtered, is that in many instances the owner of a herd would lose the work of a lifetime in building up blood, lines >in pure-bred herds. Such owners-the Pure Bred Breeders'- association-would approve calf vaccination, realizing that it is the only insurance against the disease. We admit that this is being done by some herd owners at their own expense, but where they are surrounded by careless farmers, their effort is nullified. The scheme I propose would be of value to the whole country in eliminating the disease.
I should like to quote from the Ayrshire Digest of October 15, 1942, which describes a 47696-195J
new law in force in the state of Connecticut, where compulsory vaccination of calves has been adopted. The article reads:
With the passage of a law that virtually requires compulsory vaccination of all calves except members of herds that are enrolled in the so-called test and slaughter plan, the state of Connecticut has undoubtedly put into effect the most revolutionary of all Bang's legislation. The new 'Connecticut bill was "born with teeth," for it specifies that any person refusing to have his calves vaccinated shall not be permitted to move any of his cattle from his premises except for slaughter-purposes, unless such cattle react negatively to a state approved blood test for Bang's disease. The foregoing statement practically places an embargo on movement of cattle from farms that are not enrolled in either calfhood vaccination or the test and slaughter plan. In fact in order to move cattle that -are not under one or the other of Connecticut's two plans, it is necessary to send them to slaughter or to spend time and money in testing, and with no prospects of indemnity in the event that they react.
Apparently 'Connecticut authorities are ambitious to establish Bang's control measures that may be given state-wide adoption.
Theirs is a programme for the masses and should prove to be in direct contrast to the results attained in many states where millions of dollars have been spent by owners and governments without appreciably reducing the hazards of this costly disease.
The first step toward popularizing calfhood vaccination was made when astute legislators of the "Nutmeg" state wrote into their bill the statement, "calves shall be vaccinated at state expense by an -approved licensed veterinarian who shall he assigned by the commissioner." The foregoing sentence is preceded by the following, "the commissioner of domestic animals shall cause all calves to be vaccinated against Bang's disease when they are between the -ages of four sand eight months, except calves in those herds under the state and federal cooperative herd test plan also known as test and slaughter method, which calves need not. be vaccinated -unless the owner desires." The foregoing includes these boiled-down directives that should go a long way toward developing a state-wide programme; first, the "commissioner shall cause all calves to be vaccinated," 'and second, "calves shall be vaccinated -at state expense."
The majority of the herds in Connecticut have not been tested, so to continue the plan Connecticut's new legislation will discourage private vaccination of calves for the simple reason that privately vaccinated animals will have no official status. The reason for this is their feeling that the injection of vaccine was rendered impotent because of exposure or careless handling. It was not properly, done. From fifty to sixty of Connecticut's practising local veterinarians will be employed in the work, for which an appropriation of $125,000 has been made.
I suggest that we bring this matter under discussion, and from my own knowledge of it I think that something will have to be done. about it in this country. The disease is.

I thank the hon. member for Lanark for having given as complete a review of this disease and its effects as he has. He knows the problem better than those of us who are not so closely associated with it, but I may say that a great deal is being done. Let me mention one fact to substantiate that statement. We do know, if we look back to the days prior to the war, that the general economic condition of the world played havoc with our sense of security. Trade usually results in bringing about a better understanding between the nations of * the world and in promoting friendships. We are usually more friendly with those with whom we trade. The world has grown smaller because modern means of communication have made the world a more compact, closely-knit unit. We know that the fruits of the earth are sufficient to maintain the peoples of the world, and we must seek to distribute the products of our industry, of our fields, our forests and our farms.
Reference has been made to a return to the gold standard. I do not think there is anything wrong in a return to the gold standard. The one great fault of the gold standard, as we understood it in days gone by, was that it was too rigid, but if we do return to the gold standard I have every reason to believe that it will be made more flexible. Most students of world affairs and of economics agree !hat we must have some reasonable standard of values and that it must be reasonably durable. I do not see why we should hesitate to give consideration to a return to the gold standard. In other words, may I pose this question. Suppose we were not returning to the gold standard while the great powers of the world were seeking to do so. Do you suppose we could defeat their purpose? After all, we are a gold producing nation, and I should like to see that one precious metal, one of our greatest natural' resources, used to a large extent for the benefit of the people.
When I listen to speakers addressing themselves to this problem of Bretton Woods I cannot imagine anyone holding a gun at Britain's head or attempting to force Britain to become a party to a pact if she felt that it would result in a situation such as has been indicated by hon. members of the Social Credit group. It is true that the Bretton Woods conference was held while the war was still in progress, and some have suggested that it was because of Britain's dire need that she was willing to accept the results of that conference. But many hon. members will recall that the Right Hon. Mr. Churchill, when he was Prime Minister, said in one of his memorable talks that one of the great weaknesses of the Versailles treaty was that the war had been concluded, that the allied nations had not the same things in common, and that they would have done well if they had approached the problems of peace while the war was still going; and he expressed the hope that the united nations on this occasion

would approach the problems of peace while they were still comrades in arms. I think that is one of the strongest features of this conference.
As a matter of fact, I do not think that the question of survival was in doubt; we confidently believed that sooner or later victory would be ours, though we knew that the struggle would be a long and trying one. We knew the weaknesses of the old league of nations; wre knew that it provided nothing in the way of trade to hold the nations together; we knew that there must be some compensating value for that which was being contributed. I feel therefore that Bretton Woods is an attempt at least to provide the answer, and that never again shall we be required to drench the soil of Europe in the best blood of Canada, something that has happened twice in our generation.
I do not necessarily accept the advice of the experts. I do not pose as a statistician. I am more inclined to listen to the voice of reason and to seek if possible to bring about a greater understanding, friendliness and comradeship among all peoples of the world. I believe it was Darwin who expounded the theory that like begets like, and I feel that if in a moment of ill-considered judgment or haste or concern we use harsh words to describe the attitude of our great and friendly neighbour; if in a misguided moment we seek to destroy that feeling of good will and concern that should be mutual, and which I am sure now exists, we can do a great deal of harm. We should be guarded in our language. I hope that before this debate concludes we shall have composed our differences and that when the bill goes to the banking and commerce committee any technical aspects of it that need adjustment will be attended to.
For a moment I should like hon. members to look at Europe to-day. In my opinion this is indeed the gravest moment possible in the world's history. Those people in Europe are starving. How many of us realize that a hundred thousand people still lie buried beneath the rubble of Warsaw; that five millions are homeless in Poland, living in trenches and in caves with perhaps a mere shelter over them, some roof to protect them from the elements, from the rigours of winter; that these people are very poorly clad; that disease, indeed tuberculosis, is rampant and thousands are dying? Consider the caloric content of their diet. It has been raised to 1,520 calories a day, whereas UNRRA fixed as an objective 2,250; and we know on the authority of scientists that a diet of around 1,400 is considered a starvation diet. Yet these people are existing under such terrible conditions. What is

Bretton Woods Agreements
it that keeps them alive? Merely hope; and if we do anything to destroy that hope, chaos and despair will be the lot of Europe.
It is interesting to reflect for a moment upon what the terrible realities of war have meant to that great continent. In one centre were there is located one of the largest steel industries in the world, with two hundred odd blast furnaces, only two are in operation. Why? Because in France alone ten thousand bridges are down; their railroads have been destroyed, ' huge locomotives lying over embankments; and their transportation is difficult. Indeed, they can transport only sufficient coke and coal to this huge steel industry to keep two of these furnaces going, while steel is so badly needed.
A story was told the other night which gives us an inkling of the hope and the courage of these people. A seventeen year old Yugoslav girl was looking over the ruins of her small community where between 500 and 600 persons resided before that place was destroyed. She said, through an interpreter, to a member of IJNRRA, that her parents had been killed, her family completely destroyed, and she was the only one left. "But," she said, "I will rebuild my community." She will not however rebuild that community, no matter how courageous she may be, unless we keep her from becoming a victim of disease, unless we can provide food for the sustenance of her body and the preservation of that courage which is so necessary to-day. Let me say to you, Mr. Speaker, that if the great continent of Europe, with its hundreds of millions of people, slips into the abyss of despair, people on this continent and elsewhere throughout the universe will suffer; because we have surely arrived at the point where we recognize the fact that you cannot have prosperity in one part of the world while another part is in dire stress and starving.
We should recognize and pay attention to the words of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson), who is a world traveller, and who brought a message to us last night which would indicate that the United States is approaching the period when she will be a large importer because she is gradually exhausting her natural resources.
What is needed more than anything else in this world to-day is a wave of Christianity and good sound Christian thinking, such as that which swept England during the days of John Wesley, when that country stood at the very door of paganism. From that great period came Lord Shaftesbury, the emancipator of labour, who sought to remove children from -the industrial slums and to have women return to their homes. I hope the time is not 47696-196
too far distant when in this country and in other lands women will recognize that woman's highest ideal indeed is that of motherhood. I also think of Dr. Barnardo, the father of fatherless children.
To-day we stand at the crossroads. We, and we alone, can determine our future course. We shall never build a world society if we allow our minds to inject into our thoughts suspicion, doubt and discord. Our hope for civilization is a world at peace for a long time, so that civilization will have an opportunity to rebuild those moral forces, to strengthen its courage. With that determination we can indeed approach the future with confidence.
We are citizens of the world, citizens of the world society. When Bretton Woods was presented to this house I had hope that at least Canada, one of the great trading nations of the world with much to gain-I do not want to use that language in a selfish sense, because I hope that we shall be big enough to share our prosperity with the world; we have too much at stake to do otherwise-would give unanimous endorsation to the pact and that at least we might try to bring abotu a semblance of orderly trade and exchange. I do not believe we can do that without having some central clearing house, and I have confidence enough in this pact to believe that Bretton Woods will provide just exactly that. Therefore I say to hon. members, let us not be hasty in our judgment.
I recently read a statement of Mr. Attlee, the present Prime Minister of Great Britain, in which he said that Great Britain desired to have friendly relations with all nations of the world and to know their neighbours better. I cannot feel that those who were inspired to bring about this approach to world problems were entirely guided by selfish motives and ideals, because I believe that the great war has taught us a tremendous lesson. Society on all levels have lived together in Great Britain in trying circumstances and have grown to appreciate each other more and more. It is for us in our generation to be big enough and broad enough in our vision that our children and our children's children will find that we indeed have kept alive that hope, that we have lit a new beacon which will shine and encourage future generations not to copy our example, our hatred and warfare, but to copy our example of bringing about as rapidly as possible the ideals of the brotherhood of man that we in this country. can particularly understand and appreciate.
I am satisfied that given the opportunity to survive, great good can come from Bretton

But let us at least seize this opportunity to give effect to something which has a semblance of hope, a degree of understanding and an approach to the world's' problem of deciding our future course, in the hope that there will come peace and security to a tried war-torn and troubled world.

Mr. Speaker, I do not lay any claim to being an expert, either amateur or professional, on international exchange, foreign trade or kindred matters. I do not believe that one needs to be an expert to pass judgment on the subject now before the house. If one has an understanding of the simple elementary principles which operate in the economics of the countries of the world, it is a sufficient guide to one to indicate whether the measure is sound or unsound. I agree that the Bretton Woods agreement involves all the iniquities referred to by my colleagues who have already spoken; but in addition to that, this whole scheme is nothing less than a red herring to distract the attention of the peoples of the various countries of the world from the real issue. It is a scapegoat for the sins, not only of omission but of commission, of the various'governments of the world. No international organization framed along the lines of Bretton Woods and designed under present circumstances can bring about vrorld prosperity. All these schemes for international organizations, Bretton Woods and any others, are based on. a false premise. Unless the premise on which any organization is based is sound and true, then the organization which is built upon it cannot serve the needs of humanity.
The conditions to which the minister referred, which prevailed in the pre-war days and which have been mentioned frequently by practically all hon. members who have spoken thus far, were not causes; they were effects. The minister stated, at page 3041 of Hansard:
The characteristic features of world economic relationships before the war were high and discriminatory tariffs, import quotas, export subsidies, depreciated currencies of uncertain value, discriminatory clearing agreements, multiple currency practices.
It is true that those conditions prevailed, but I assert that they were symptoms of the disease and not the disease itself; they were effects, not causes. I think the most convincing proof that tariff arrangements or any kind of trade relationships which may be suggested will not bring about prosperity may be found in what has taken place in the United States of America. There we have a

union consisting of forty-eight states. There are no tariff barriers between them, no inhibitions to trade, no obstacles, nothing in the way of the freest possible exchange.

speechtext: They have the same money, too; stabilized money.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
They have almost everything that is required to bring about the greatest possible prosperity within the boundaries of that nation. They have a common language; they have one money system common to all. Yet in the pre-war days they suffered from the depression as much as any other country in the world, if not more. If adjustments in tariffs or the abolition of tariffs and the elimination of all these other things to which the minister referred as the causes of depression are the cure, then why was there a depression in the United States, when these things were absent from its internal organization? So I say the conditions and circumstances referred to by the minister and by other hon. members are the symptoms of disease and not the cause; and the thing we must do is to discover and eliminate the cause. Then the symptoms will take care of themselves.
In my opinion Bretton Woods will fail, and so will every other similar organization that may be attempted, because they are based upon a false premise. What is that false premise to which I refer? Why has there been and why is there now again suggested this constant drive for foreign markets? On every side we. hear that we must export, export, export. What has been the reason that the exporters in various countries of the world have agitated so strongly for exports? Simply because they believe that the people within the country either do not desire the goods or cannot consume them. The whole drive for foreign markets is predicated on the assumption that the people at home either do not wish the goods or are not physically able to consume them, and I say that is a false premise. It is true that those who have referred to foreign trade in this debate have said that trade must be a two-way street, that it must work both ways; but the mere exchange of goods between one nation and another does not guarantee that the people of those countries will be able to enjoy the goods when they receive them. The chief reason that the people of Canada desire to export-and this is true of the people of the United States and almost every country in the world-is not the fact that they do not desire the ^oods, but it.is largely that they are unable to purchase them. In days gone by many articles have been exported by Canada that we could

Bretton TToods Agreements
have consumed here if we had possessed sufficient purchasing power, and the same would apply to every country in the world.
I have before me a page from the Canada Year Book giving the statistics in regard to Canada's exports for the year 1938-39. I readily grant that we produce many commodities in Canada which we could not hope physically to consume, but we have also exported many things which Canadians would have been glad to enjoy themselves if they had possessed sufficient purchasing power. These items are arranged in order of importance, and I notice that the sixth most important export at that time was planks, boards and lumber, which we exported to the amount of $37,000,000. We all know that in those days prior to the war, as is the case now, many people would have bought that lumber if they had been able to do so. One only needs to take a trip across this country to discover the tremendous need that exists for new buildings. We could have used every stick of that lumber in this country. The next item in the list is meats. I am not suggesting that Canadians could physically consume all the meat products we produce, but there are many people in this country who would gladly avail themselves of much greater quantities of steaks, hams and all the other meats that are processed in this country if they had the ability to purchase them. People cannot afford to eat many steaks at a cost of $1.25 or $1.50 per meal. So I say that in pre-war days as well as post-war days we could consume in Canada far more of the commodities we produce in this country.
I see that automobiles are eleventh in -this list of twenty-five items; in that year we exported 58,S49 automobiles. What in the name of common sense are we exporting automobiles for when there are so many people in this country without automobiles and a great many more running around in worn out jalopies tied up with haywire? So one could go all the way down the line. In the past we have exported products which could very well have been consumed here at home, and I say the reason they were not so consumed was not that -the people did not desire them, but purely and simply that their purchasing power was not equal to their producing power. I have already said that it seems to be taken for granted on the part of those who are constantly talking about foreign trade that if we export a million dollars worth of commodities and then bring back in exchange a million dollars worth of commodities the people will be automatically able to buy those imported goods. That is 47696-196J
a false assumption. A word as to the reason why it is false, why the premise on which I claim the whole scheme is based is a false one.
One of the objectives which it is hoped to attain through the use of the Bretton Woods agreement and many other measures which have been adopted, both national and international, is the achievement of what is described as full employment. The minister stated several times in his address that that is an objective they are hoping to achieve. The term has been used frequently, indeed incessantly during debates in this house and, doubtless, elsewhere: we must "cure unemployment". I wish to challenge that contention. There is only way that unemployment in this modern world, this power-machine age, will ever be cured, and that is by setting up a slave state. Personally I do not want to see unemployment cured. Unemployment is not a disease. It is the greatest sign of progress which we have yet witnessed.

Unemployment is a sign of progress and not a sign of decay. It has faced this country and it will face us again.
Statistics were quoted by an hon. member of this group, yesterday I believe, indicating that the United States is expecting 20,900,000 unemployed by the time the reconversion period is over. I am satisfied that that will be the condition in every country in the world, particularly in those countries which have the greatest development in technology. The reason for this unemployment must be obvious to everyone; yet it is ignored , continuously. Not only do hon. members and economists who talk and write on the subject ignore the fact that we have been and are now in a power-machine massrproduction age, but they ignore the fact that we have now entered the atomic age. The unemployment which prevailed prior to the war and which will occur again, once we get through the reconversion period, is merely technological; it indicates that man has used his head to save his back, and I think he is entitled to do that. Personally, subscribing to the philosophy that I do, I do not want to see unemployment cured, I want to see more unemployed.

That does not mean that those who have that ambition desire to loaf; it means simply that they desire to reach a position where they can choose their activity instead of being forced to take it. That is the difference between work and leisure. I say that it is a false objective to endeavour to cure unemployment by providing work either nationally or internationally. What is the difference between that philosophy and the philosophy which Adolf Hitler followed? I see no difference.
I say that Bretton Woods will fail because nations, governments and those who speak on behalf of governments fail to recognize the impact of the power-machine age and-now- the advent of atomic energy. More and more we shall have power-machine production, and eventually the application of atomic energy when it is commercially feasible. When extraneous energy displaces human labour, it displaces the pay cheque; and when it displaces the pay check, obviously people have not purchasing power to buy the goods which machines make. Hence has arisen the drive to export those goods whjch would otherwise in large measure be consumed right at home. I believe this truth must be recognized by governments and those who speak on their behalf before we shall make any progress either in preserving peace in the world or in bringing about prosperity. We certainly shall have peace in the world only after we learn how to distribute our abundances. The greatest contribution which we as Canadians could make to the cause of peace would be to demonstrate how we can distribute our abundances here at home without mortgaging the lives of those now living, or the lives of future Canadians, to those who issue the money of the nation. If we can demonstrate how it is possible to distribute our own goods and avoid economic warfare with other
(Mr. J. L. Gibson.]
countries then I consider we shall be making the greatest contribution that Canada can make.
I assert that Canadians have the first claim to Canadian goods. All goods produced in Canada are produced with Canadian labour and by Canadian effort. Therefore Canadians have the first claim on Canadian production. Once we have passed through the transitional period, I am not in favour of exporting a single article until Canadians are first satisfied completely. I agree that during the transitional period we have a moral obligation to rehabilitate those countries which have been overrun by the enemy, but as my colleague, the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) indicated, this should be an outright gift and should not constitute a debt. I repeat that we as Canadians should rehabilitate the war-stricken countries of the world with some of the superabundance of goods that we have. But once they have been rehabilitated, once their machinery of production is brought back to the place where they themselves can provide almost all the things they need, we shall then be faced with the problem of disposing of our so-called surplus. That makes it imperative that all countries, particularly the United States and Canada, should institute within their countries a system which will enable the people at home to consume to the maximum of their own goods.
I assert that we must eventually come to the place where we accept one of the major proposals in the social credit philosophy, the bonusing of consumers or, in other words, a national dividend. I do not propose on this occasion to elaborate on that; but I am convinced that only by a national bonus, only by increasing the ability of the consumer to buy his own production, and that which may be brought in in exchange for genuine surpluses, can we ever bring about prosperity of a substantial nature. An hon. member over here has said that if is a case of Bretton Woods or chaos. I would suggest another slogan-a national dividend or chaos.

Yes, definitely. Taxes decrease rather than increase the purchasing power. I shall not be satisfied until all taxation is abolished. Those who think that taxation is necessary simply do not understand the a-b-c's of the relationship of money to goods. It is assumed constantly that consumption always equals production, but that is the greatest fallacy that can be assumed by any one. As long as we in Canada assume that when we produce a billion dollars worth of

Bretton Woods Agreements
goods we automatically have a billion dollars of purchasing power we shall make absolutely no progress. On previous occasions I have shown by statistics, and anyone can demonstrate it by examining the books of his own business, that in every business of this country there is only approximately half as much distributed in purchasing power as is produced. The thing we need is an increase in purchasing power, not a redistribution of it, and that is why I say that taxation should be abolished.
Even under a system where we enable the consumer to acquire up to the limits of his capacity to consume of our own production, I grant that there will be genuine surpluses which we can not physically consume. Those would be available for export. To-day when we have a surplus, whether genuine or not, we think immediately of exporting it. I think the reverse should be the case. When we have a genuine surplus, whether it be wheat or newsprint or aluminum or any other commodity, and we have satisfied Canadian consumers to the limit, we should import an equivalent amount from the other countries of the world.
By following that process we would put in an order to other countries for goods of an equivalent amount. Will they be ready and, willing to sell to us? Of course they will. That would turn the wheels of industry in those countries and thus generate purchasing power which would enable them to put in orders for our surplus. In that way trade wars would be overcome, or at least we would be doing our part to eliminate such trade wars. When those goods come into Canada, let us s,ee to it that the Canadian consumer has sufficient purchasing power to acquire them. Merely [DOT]exchanging goods, merely bringing back- one surplus in exchange for another, will not automatically guarantee distribution. As I have already said, we must tackle the question of distribution within our own country and .consider it the fundamental basis of the success of any international arrangement.
If that is done it will mean that those who now have a stranglehold on this nation and other nations of the world will have to give up some of their powers. To-day the economy of Canada is absolutely in the hands of those who create and issue money. Those who create and issue the money of the nation control the nation; the government does not. The government is helpless to effect any vital changes in the economy of the country as long as the power to create and issue the money of the nation is in the hands of private individuals. Before any country, whether it be Canada, the United States or any other, is in
a position to enable its own people to consume its own production, it must first restore to the crown its most sacred prerogative, that of creating and issuing the money of the nation.
By that I do not mean that I favour the nationalization of the chartered banks, because I do not. I believe that when the government goes into the banking business the people will be obliged to do business with politicians instead of with business men. I want to see the private banks remain in private hands so that business men may do business with business men, and not with politicians. But the power to create and issue the money which the banks now enjoy must be taken from them and restored to the crown, and then the crown must use that privilege on behalf of the people to; enable the people to consume their own production without adding to the debt and without an increase in taxation.

I was asserting, Mr. Speaker, that if we are to make Bretton Woods a success we must ia Canada restore to the crown the powers which will enable it to enable the people to consume their own production; that is, we must restore to the crown the power to create and issue the money of the nation. In this connection I should like to quote a statement made by Abraham Lincoln, who said:
Money is the creature of law, and the creation of the original issue of money should be maintained as an exclusive monopoly of the national government. Such needs can be served by issuing national currency and credit through the operation of a national banking system.
The government should create, issue, and circulate all the currency and credit needed to satisfy the spending power of the government and the buying power of consumers. The privilege of creating and issuing money is not only the^ supreme prerogative of the government, but it is the government's greatest creative opportunity.
That is a statement of great significance. That is what should be done in Canada; that is what should be done in the United States; that is what should be done in every country; and until that is done, and until that privilege is used, by the state for the benefit of the '

people, Bretton Woods will not succeed in bringing about prosperity or peace in the world.
I consider that the refusal by those who are responsible to restore to the crown its sacred prerogative constitutes one of the greatest betrayals that have ever been made of the people of this country or of any country in the world, and my suspicion is this in connection with Bretton. Woods. My colleague the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansel!) on various occasions has suggested the operation of a power behind the scenes. I concur in his fear of this power. Yes; what about the others? It is a' strange thing that in a debate of this importance, that while the two major parties have been at one another's throats during the session, this is, one might say, quite a love feast. I do not think there will be found much disagreement between them on this occasion. Not only is it a love feast, but one might say that they are actually dining off the gold plate. The minister said yesterday that no country was willing to revert to the gold standard. More than that, he said that prosperity, that is national prosperity, depends on export, trade, and he also said that export trade will be controlled by gold. That is definite enough, so that our prosperity will be controlled by gold.
Mention has been made of tariffs, and governments are always blamed for raising tariffs out of pure cussedness. It never seems to penetrate these people that tariffs are not a cause but a result. As a previous speaker said, it is because no industrialist country can afford to consume its own production, nor can it afford to consume the production of other countries in exchange for its own, and therefore in order to defend themselves they put on a tariff so as to export as much as possible and import as little as possible. In other

Bretton Woods Agreements
words, they export their unemployment. That is so elementary that I apologize for mentioning it at this time.	'[DOT]
We are told that all the experts were agreed. I do not know that that is very remarkable. No doubt they were all hand-picked and had already agreed; otherwise they would not have gone there.

speechtext: Agreed beforehand.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Yes; and who are the experts? Most of them, those who Were used are the product of the London School of Economics, a socialist college or school of which the presiding genius at the present time is Professor Lasky. That college is responsible for the experts whom you people over there, who pride yourselves on being Liberals, are going to vote to support. I do not know whether hon. members have read Hayek's "Road to Serfdom." Here I should like to acknowledge an unknown benefactor. I did mention this book at the beginning of the session. I quoted from the "Road to Serfdom" and suggested that it would be a good thing if every member of the house would read it. A few days afterwards' a copy was sent to me, and I understand that every member in the house received one as well. I do not know who sent it, but whoever he is I take this opportunity of thanking him. He is a generous man, and a great benefactor if the book has been read.
The London School of Economics was founded fifty or sixty years ago by Fabian socialists in London, and some time before the last war it was endowed with some five million dollars by the.late Sir Ernest Oassel, .the German international financier. When asked by Lord Haldane why he had bestowed those millions on this college he said his reason was that it was the purpose of the London School of Economics to train the bureaucracy of the future wrorld socialist state. That is the purpose of the college, and that school has turned out a stream of economists, gold-plated economists, and subversive professors who have taught the youth of the empire to lose faith in the empire and in our power to govern ourselves as free peoples. And that work still goes on, and Bretton Woods is one rotten egg that has come out of that school, whether you believe it or not.
I do not pose as an expert, so may I quote Mr. Smith, congressman from Ohio, speaking in the United States congress in 1943 with reference to Bretton Woods. He said.
We are apt to be led to believe from the newspapers, radio and other reports that this scheme emanates from a few individuals. Mir. Harry D. White, special assistant to the secretary of the treasury, is being credited as the prime mover
of the United States contribution to the plan. Professor Maynard Keynes is being credited as the prime mover of the British contribution to this plan. Now, of course, we would be naive indeed if we were to believe that the officials of our treasury had undertaken this task on their own initiative or that Professor Keynes and perhaps a few of his associates had inaugurated their part of the scheme on their own accord. We may rest assured that back of this move are the most powerful international monied interests and financiers of the world. Furthermore, we may be certain that world power politics are playing a prominent role in promoting this movement.
I should now like to quote a man against whom I do not think anybody in this house will have much to say, namely, the Right Hon. Winston Churchill. I shall not apologize for quoting him. How are we to judge an expert except by the results of his expert advice? By their fruits ye shall know them. Listen to Mr. Churchill. In the House of Commons in 1932, as a private member he said this. I shall not read it all. He reminded the house that in 1925 when he was the chancellor of the exchequer he took the advice of the highest experts, men of great ability, indisputable integrity and sincerity, to the effect, that if they returned to the gold standard they would anchor themselves to stability and reality. He accepted their advice and he went on to say:
I take for myself and my colleagues of other days whatever degree of blame and burden there may be for having accepted their advice. But what has happened? We have had no reality, no stability. The price of gold has risen since then by more than seventy per cent. That is as if a twelve-inch footrule had suddenly been stretched to nineteen or twenty inches; as if the pound avoirdupois weight had suddenly become twenty-three to .twenty-four ounces. Look at what this has meant to everybody who has been compelled to execute their contracts upon this irrationally enhanced scale. Look at the gross unfairn^s of such a distortion to all producers of new wealth, and to all that labour and science and enterprise can give us. Minor fluctuations might well be ignored but I say quite seriously that this monetary convulsion has now reached a pitch where I am persuaded that the producers of new wealth will not tolerate indefinitely so hideous an oppression.
The man who made that statement was man enough to admit his mistakes; he, more than any one man, saved the world in 1940. I think we would do well to-day to listen to what he said then. He said that he was advised by the best experts, men of undoubted integrity and ability. He took their advice, and what- happened? Chaos and ruin. It is not too much to say that it was one of the main causes of the late war. And now we are going to do the same thing again. We have the same lot of experts who, have never apologized and have never admitted their mistakes.
Bretton Woods Agreements

I should like to go back a couple of years to a personal experience in this House of Commons. In 1943 I was speaking on international financial policies and the discussion turned to gold. I made the statement that eighty-five per cent of the gold under Fort Knox in the United States was owned or controlled by private interests. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) was in his place, as he is to-day. He took exception to my statement and said:
I should like to correct one misstatement of fact by the hon. gentleman. He said he would stake his reputation on the statement that eighty-five per cent of all the gold at Fort Knox was owned by private interests, and not by the
fovernment of the United States. I have sent or the federal reserve bulletin of July, 1943, and the annual report of the secretary of the treasury on the state of the finances for the fiscal year ending 'June 30. 1942. At page 638 of the federal reserve bulletin I find a table headed: "Analysis of changes in gold stock of the United States," from which I find that in June, 1942, the stock of the United States of America was $22,737,000,000 odd.
His final statement was:
The records are prefectly clear, that the gold stock of the United States is owned an- its entirety by the United States treasury.
Is the ministe'r equally sure to-day as he was when he made that statement? I staked my reputation on my statement. Is the minister equally sure to-day as he was then that all the gold under Fort Knox is owned in its entirety by the government? I should like the minister to answer that question.

It does not say that the
same thing is an asset and a liability. It says that the gold certificates are liabilities, and the gold is an asset.
