speechtext:
Well, on page 63S it gives the stock of money in the United States as $35 billion; but the amount held for federal reserve banks and agents is $17,750 million. It is just as though an elevator contains 100,000 bushels of wheat. There is the wheat, all right, but 80,000 bushels have been deposited by farmers who have grain certificates against it. I think that is the real position of the gold in the United States. I mention that because I consider it to be of fundamental importance. People get the idea that Bretton Woods will be all right because the people own the gold. I maintain that the people do not own the gold; they do not control it. Of course, when my colleagues and I criticize the policies of the United States, both their financial policy and their anti-British policy, it is understood that we are not criticizing the people of the United States at all, because they are perfectly innocent and, I may -add, largely ignorant of what is going on.
When I was in England the winter before last I put a question to an authority there, whose name I am not at liberty to mention in public because this was a private conversation, but I am perfectly certain that no hon. member would question his knowledge, and if they are - interested I should be pleased to give his name in private. I asked this gentleman if he had happened to read a certain debate, which I mentioned, in the Canadian House of Commons, and lie said that he had. I said, "Well, was I right or wrong?" He replied "Jaques, you were absolutely right; there is no question about that." I said, "Well, if I was absolutely right, how do you account for the fact that the minister must have been wrong?" His reply was, " I am quite certain that the statement was not made to deceive anybody, but he just did not know." So that even the experts do not know; that is the position.
I should now like to go back to the year 1943. In April of that year a Mr. Sandwell addressed a meeting of the league of nations society somewhere in this city, and according to the report which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen the next day he predicted a supranational authority with power to settle questions of immigration, natural resources, the protection of minorities, the repudiation of debt, finance and other questions. Then he went on to say that the loyalty of Canadians must be weaned away from the crown to an authority wider than Canada, wider than the empire and wider even than democracy. I

Bretton Woods Agreements
thought that was something which should not have been, said, especially in war time, and I brought it to the attention of the house on a question of privilege. Immediately I was assailed in the press right across Canada and called every name they could print. I was accused of wasting the time of the House of Commons. Particularly was I assailed by the Winnipeg Free Press. A week later there appeared a dispatch from Washington, as follows:
Secretary Henry Morgenthau disclosed to-day comprehensive administration plans to stabilize post-war currencies and fix their value in -terms of gold. The plans involve:
1.	Creation of ap international stabilization fund by the united nations and their associates.
2.	Fixing the value of currencies in terms of gold.
3.	An agreement -among participating countries not to devalue their currencies without consulting other members of the stabilization fund.
Both plans entail the establishment of a stabilization fund to be managed by an international bank, vitally important because it would mean that participating counti-res would -lose control over the value of their currencies for world trade purposes. This control would be vested in the bank, not in a parliament or a congress, and if a country wanted the rate .lowered or increased it could only appeal to the bank, not take action itself.
That was the first intimation of the Bretton Woods plan, and t^ie speaker at the meeting of the league of nations society here in Ottawa prepared the way for it by telling the people they would have to surrender their loyalty to the crown. In other words, they would have to surrender their sovereignty, and to what? To international bankers and the gold standard. Is that what we fought the war for? It is not what I rose in my place in this house in 1939 to support.

speechtext: Our boys did not die for that, either.	[DOT]

speechtext:
No. What about the Atlantic charter? We do Dot hear much about that to-day. Let me refer to a recent debate in the British House of Commons, when they were discussing conditions in Europe at the present time. One hon. member said that instead of the united nations charter, "since Potsdam something different has been- added; we are contracting into a country very little larger than the United Kingdom over sixty million people. It appears that something like the , fiendish Morgenthau plan is i being carried out." Who is this Mr. Morgenthau? He is a former secretary of the United States treasury and connected with Kuhn, Loeb and other international bankers. He is also the sponsor of the international monetary plans agreed to at Bretton Woods. It was these
same international bankers who financed Japan's war against Russia in 1904 and German and Japanese rearmament for the second world war, while the British empire and America were kept in a state of depression and unpreparedness. Now, according to the Morgenthau plan, war-tom Europe is to be weakened by division, starvation, hardship and the liquidation of democratic leadership until reduced to a Balkan standard of living, and eastern Europe will be added to the "new democracies" within the power-complex orbit of the Soviet Union.
I should like to refer to an article published in a well-known magazine by Doctor Ludwig von Mises. We are told at the end of the article that Doctor Ludwig von Mises was recently professor of international economic relations at the graduate institute of international studies at Geneva, previously professor of economics at the university of Vienna, and author of "Socialism". Speaking of international finance between the two wars, he makse this statement:
The state of things which -prevailed in the last decades can be characterized -as a complete surrender of the rights of the creditors and of the investors. Every nation successfully made use of its sovereignty to the disadvantage of foreign creditors and investors. Every nation exercised its power to expropriate foreign investments directly or indirectly by discriminatory taxation, to debase the currency, with which loans had to be repaid. The history of international financial relations has, in the last twenty years, been one of almost continual embezzlement-. The governments of the debtor countries behaved like swindlers for the benefit of their own treasury and for the benefit of pressure groups within their population.
The new covenant of the -league of nations- %
One might say that instead of the league of nations we have got Dumbarton Oaks and Bretton Woods and the united nations.
-will therefore have to include -a rigid limitation on the sovereign rights of every nation. Unilateral measures which -affect the essentials of the contractual obligations, the currency system, taxation and other important matters have to be rendered unlawful. The debtor countries should not have any rights which -are denied to private debtors.
And he went on to say:
All these provisions will have to be efficiently enforced by international tribunals and by sanctions which the league must -apply with a greater measure of success than in the past. Without some kind of international police power such a plan could not be carried out. Coercive measures are indispensable in order to make reluctant debtor countries pay.
We have had Mr. Churchill's statement about the doubling of the debts by the gold standard, and, as a consequence, the impossible conditions in which the debtor nations found themselves. Now, under this scheme, under
Bretton Woods Agreements

Dumbarton Oaks, under the united nations set-up, it is suggested that we should'have an international police force. You can see the beauty of the scheme. First of all you put the world on a gold standard so as to double and treble the debts, and then, when private individuals and countries find it impossible to carry out their contractual obligations, the bailiff will enter the country and will be supported by an international police.

speechtext:
Yes, and atomic bombs.
Speaking of atomic bombs and the activities of experts generally, both financial and other experts, I believe it is a good time to say that experts should be on tap, not on top. It is the experts who produced the atomic bomb. Is it the experts who are to tell us when to drop it, and on whom? That does not lie with experts. It does not need experts' advice; it needs only common honesty, which the vast majority of people have and would apply rightly if only they knew the truth.
Speaking locally, I have in my hand a little pamphlet setting out the farmers' action programme of the Alberta Farmers' Union and the United Farmers of Canada (Saskatchewan section). Most farmers are familiar with it.
I am going to quote only three or four lines on page 6 under the heading "Financial Policy":
The people of Canada must have complete control of the nation's money system which must be operated under the direction of parliamentary policy with a national finance committee in charge, under the chairmanship of a person who shall have the power of a judge of a superior court.	[DOT]
I put this question to every hon. member in this house': Under the provisions of this act of Bretton Woods, if it is adopted, will the people of Canada have complete control of the nation's monetary policy? That is the question hon,. members have to decide when they come to vote on this proposal. Are they going to vote for these ideas of internationalism, international government, international controls, or are they going to vote for the people who sent them to this place? That is the decision we have to make. It is a decision which I have already made, or I would not be speaking this afternoon.
A word about gold mining. I cannot help thinking-and in saying this I am not attributing anything in the nature of dishonest motives-that most of the speakers who have defended the Bretton Woods proposals are speaking on behalf of the gold mining industry of Canada. I repeat that I do not attribute improper motives at all; perhaps the 
majority, or an important section, of the constituents of some hon. members are themselves gold miners. Mention has been made, quite recently by the last Progressive Conservative member who addressfid the house, of the tragic and terrible conditions which exist at this moment in the greater part of Europe. We are officially told by Sir John Orr, who, I believe, is president of the united nations food organization, that more people will die this winter in Europe from starvation and hardship than were killed in the whole six years of war. Of those who preach the virtues of gold mining in this country as a means of producing employment and wealth, I would ask: How much food, how many clothes, and how much shelter will all the gold in the world produce for those people? Can they eat it? Can they wear it? Can they warm themselves with it? There it is, down in a hole in the ground, absolutely useless; yet we go on mining more and more gold, under the delusion that by doing so we are getting rich. If lunacy can go farther, I do not know in what direction.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister will no doubt have gathered, the Social Credit group is definitely opposed to any gold standard, camouflaged or otherwise. Gold has never reflected the real wealth of any nation, or of the world for that matter. I believe it would be well to define what is meant by wealth. We in this group believe that wealth is goods and services provided to the people when and if required. To us gold has the same meaning as any other metal which might be used in the making of rings, jewellery and so forth, and it should sell for about $2 an ounce and no more.
Yesterday the minister made a good speech in presenting the case for Bretton Woods, but in making his statement I think he was perhaps too confident of the success of this measure. I think he felt that it would go through without any opposition or perhaps without any discussion. In his presentation he made this statement:
In the measure now before it, the house is asked to express its approval of Canadian participation in the two new international financial institutions considered at the united nations monetary and financial conference held at Bretton Woods.
Let me repeat what he said, "The house is asked to express its approval." Apparently he did not think the house might not care to approve the measure; he took it for granted that it would approve. Even though he may be right, I still think the minister should have said that these proposals were placed

Bretton Woods Agreements
before this house for approval or disapproval. That is the stand I take. Then he went on to say:
The proposed institutions are intended to be part of the permanent framework of international collaboration in the monetary field.
In. the next column he continues and says:
The main issue which is at stake in the Bretton Woods proposals is the same as that involved in the united nations charter which this house recently approved by so overwhelming a majority. That issue is: Are we and other countries to organize and cooperate for peace?
Then he continues a little farther on:
In many parts of the world there is evident a keen awareness that if peace is to be maintained and if prosperity is to be achieved it will be necessary to plan for a higher degree of international collaboration than we have ever achieved in peace time in the past. In pursuit of this purpose, the united nations are in process of creating a number of institutions which are to serve as the instruments of such collaboration. The central institution is, of course, the united nations organization embodied in the San Francisco charter. This, it is hoped, will provide the political basis of security. But it is recognized that security also has an economic basis and that economic instability and poverty and unemployment provide a background conducive to political dissension among nations.
In other words, the minister chose to present this measure by way of making an appeal for the promotion of peace. I happen to have been looking over some of the statements which have appeared in various publications, and I find that this propaganda has been going on for some time, certainly since the beginning of the war. The words used' are practically identical with those used by the Minister of Finance in speaking to this motion. I find that the supporters of the so-cafled "Union Now" or federal union also claimed that we must have peace at any price. They asked the nations of the world to subscribe *o the establishment of an international government and to relinquish their national sovereignty. This international government was to have control over, first, the monetary policies of the countries in the union; second, the armed forces of the countries in the union; 'hird, an international police force; fourth, citizenship rights of the people in the union; fifth, postal and other means of communication and, sixth, the regulation of foreign and other trade. It is rather striking that the approach they used is almost identical to the one used by the Minister of Finance in dealing with this peace problem so-called. The minister continues and says:
The international monetary fund is primarily concerned with securing orderly exchange arrangements, while the bank is intended to help in the restoration of economies which have
been destroyed or disrupted in the course of the war and, over the longer period, to encourage and facilitate the international flow of capita] for productive investment.
I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the "Voice of Austria," published in August, 1941, in New York. The author of the article is Ludwig von Mises, who is described in the publication as being a recent professor of international studies at Geneva, a previous professor of economics at the university of Vienna and the author of "Socialism and Economic Analysis." The article says: ... if there is any hope at all that foreign capital can be procured for the post-war reconstruction of Europe, then a new legal system for the safeguarding of these investments and loans is essential. No country which stubbornly wishes to maintain its full sovereignty in this field can expect to attract foreign capital.
Do not the two statements read very much alike? Let me read what the minister said:
The international monetary fund is primarily concerned with securing orderly exchange arrangements, while the bank is intended to help in the restoration of economies which have been destroyed or disrupted in the course of the war and, over the longer period, to encourage and facilitate the international flow of capital for productive investment.
The article in. the "Voice of- Austria" continues:
The new covenant of the league of nations will therefore have to include a rigid limitation on the sovereign rights of every nation, which intends to borrow abroad or to obtain foreign investments. Unilateral measures which affect the essentials of the contratcual obligations, the currency system, taxation and other important matters have to be rendered unlawful. The debtor countries should not have any rights which are denied to private debtors. No country should have the right to inflict harm on foreign investors.
All these provisions will have to be efficiently enforced by international tribunals and by sanctions which the league must apply with a greater measure of success than in the past. Without some kind of international police power, such *a plan could not be carried out. Coercive measures are indispensable in order to make reluctant debtor countries pay.	_ _
Of course, this is equivalent to a very rigid limitation on national sovereignty. But there is no other way to make international _ capital transfers possible again. The nations involved will have to choose between the renunciation of the aid of foreign -capital or this -abandonment of their unlimited sovereign powers.
It appears to me that the whole crossword puzzle is gradually being -put together piece by piece. Parts of this scheme are embodied in various bills and presented to parliaments of the various democratic countries of the world. Of course they are made to appear very innocent and humanitarian in purpose. But these measures are being put through,
Bret ton Woods Agreements

and eventually we shall wake up one morning to find ourselves rounded up and with a wofld police force on the throne.
The Minister of Finance said:
On the political side, the keystone in the structure of institutions being set up for this purpose is the united nations charter. On the economic side we have, to date, three main pieces.
Then he mentions as No. 1, UNRRA, the united nations organization to deal with urgent problems of relief and rehabilitation; No. 2, the food and agriculture organization, and No. 3, the Bretton Woods agreement. Then he continues:
The structure of international collaboration will be by no means complete when the fund and the bank are established.
_ Which goes to prove that the whole system is being put together piece by piece and, as I have already pointed out, we shall wake up one day and find ourselves governed by an international police force. The minister says: Nor does the establishment of a monetary framework conducive to iliber-al commercial policies in itself -assure that liberal policies will in fact be followed. For this, separate -agreement is necessary.
The -minister is promising that he will bring in further measures to complete the puzzle. All we have to do is to look over some of the utterances and writings of the men prominent ih the economic -affairs of the world to see at once what striking similarity there is between their statements. I have a clipping from the Glasgow Herald of June 19, 19411, which quotes Sir Victor Sassoon, British merchant-banker who had arrived in Los Angeles the day before, en route to Shanghai. It reads as follows:
Sir Victor Sassoon said there was no other way to stop Hitler but to form a world federation of democracies, with Britain, Canada and Australia becoming a part of the United States.
"The United States," he said, "needs Britain, Australia and Canada to consume the exports of South America.
"It is now obvious," he added, "to business men of the world that the federal alliance of Britain is so necessary that it hardly bears discussion.
"Britain must come into the democracy of the United States with full rights of statehood.
"It is also obvious that such an arrangement would mean that Britain would -relinquish her traditions and institutions of government."

Yes. I maintain that it is not in -Canada's interests to see the United Kingdom reduced to the position of a second class nation. I maintain that it is in our interests to have the British commonwealth of nations remain the strongest power in Europe. But it is evident to all, I think, that

if these schemes are successful the British people will be placed in a secondary position, or perhaps worse.
Yesterday, the minister argued with the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) that the Bretton Woods proposals perhaps did not mean a return to the gold standard. He did not say whether the Bretton Woods proposals were or were not a return to the gold standard, but he placed the onus of proof on the hon. member for Acadia. It would appear to -me that it is up to the minister to tell us defi-v nitely whether it means the gold standard or not.

speechtext: And prove it.

speechtext:
And prove it. In that connection I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Victoria Daily Times of British Columbia of January 25, 1941, written by Major A. H. Jukes, D.S.O., O.B.E.. of Victoria, B.C. He said:
What does it mean to surrender our national citizenship, our control of finance, armaments, fiscal policy and judicature, and return to the gold standard?
That is what federal union proposes we should do. In return for what? Greater economic freedom for the individual? If so, we must have safeguards.
Promises are not enough. We should know: Who sponsors it? Who pays for it? And, above all, who will benefit by its adoption?
Is this another attempt to consolidate under a new name that -age-old enemy of individual freedom, centralization of power, with its absentee ownership and control? Can we recognize in it any concealed instrument of repression? Its advocates stress its sentimental value without explaining what we stand to lose.
I maintain that it is up to the minister to pxplain what Canada stands to lose if we subscribe to these proposals, and- it is also up to the minister to explain what we would gain by accepting them. To make a general statement on the proposals, which are said to constitute the most important measure to have been introduced in this house in- many a year, and discussing them in an ordinary manner, will not be satisfactory to anyone. It does not -satisfy me at any rate.
I need hardly say that the position of this group has always -been clear in reference to monetary matters, and I should like to quote from a press release which was issued by the Hon. William Aberhart, -late premier of Alberta, two or -three years ago. Mr. Aberhart denounced the federal union -proposals, and, of course, the whole scheme as it is being put over us at the present time. This is what he had to say:
The proposals involve the federation of the British nations, the U.S.A. and other demoora-/ cies in a union under a central authority. This

Privilege-Mr. Church
central authority would have absolute control over (1) the armed forces of all the countries involved in the union, (2) finance and (3) citizenship.
Control over finance would give the central authority power over every aspect of the economic life of every country within the federation. As I have pointed out before, "those who control the things that people want control the people." So that the central authority would have absolute power over the lives of all the people, in the union.
Suppose that the people of Canada were dissatisfied with the economic conditions being imposed upon them by the operation of the union's financial system, they would be powerless to do anything about it. Control over the money system would be vested in the central authority, and it would be beyond the jurisdiction of Canada's parliament to reform it.
_ Further, suppose that conditions became intolerable in Canada. Well-the international authority would have all the armed forces under its control, so the people could do nothing about it.
This all powerful central authority, with absolute totalitarian control over the people's lives, would be .the executive of the union's legislative bodies, on which the British empire would have minority representation and Canada would be impotent, for all practical purposes. Under such conditions it is more than likely that the British people would find themselves under outside domination.
As a scheme to secure the centralization of power on a vast scale for the purpose of divesting every democratic country of its sovereignty, destroying the British empire as a commonwealth of free peoples, abolishing existing democratic constitutions and substituting an international dictatorship by the money power, the proposals of "Union Now" could not be improved upon.
I maintain, however, that any loyal British subjeot, with a love of king, country and the precious democratic rights which are our inalienable inheritance, cannot but view with revulsion and alarm the open advocacy of a scheme which would rob us of all the things we hold dear, and for the preservation of which we are engaged in a life and death struggle against the menace of totalitarianism.
The late Premier Aberhart was an outstanding student of economic and political affairs, and that is the statement he made. Mr. Speaker, may I ask you to call it six o'clock?

I see no reason why a spouse living in Quebec should expect the houses of parliament to go into action' on his or her account merely because he or she has made a bad choice in marriage. I should like to say that I personally do not know how any international control of money will assist Canada in distributing the goods and services we produce among our own people. I say that to try and pretend that we can solve great problems on a worldwide scale is pure and simple shadow-boxing, and that the practical and sensible thing to do would be first to put our own house in order and endeavour to solve our own prob-' lems within our own boundaries. Surely this nation has reached the position where the leaders of government should be able to find ways and means of distributing the goods and services which the people of Canada produce, but of course we always hear appeals and speeches telling us that the only way we can . solve our problems is to get into the world arena of international finance and tie ourselves to the gold standard and other international organizations. Strange as it may seem, since the beginning of the war, great pressure has been applied .in every field to endeavour to get us to join various international organizations. Instead of hearing speeches and discussions in this house as to ways and means of preserving democracy, we hear speeches and appeals from the government benches to tie ourselves to international organizations, because this country seems to be too small for us.	,

Bretton Woods Agreements
The slogan of this group, Mr. Speaker, is that that which is physically possible and desirable must be made financially possible. How in the world can we make everything that is physically possible and desirable financially possible within our own country if we tie ourselves to some external force or authority? The people of this nation, and particularly those who advise the government, should be in a position to find ways and means of making financially possible that which is physically possible and desirable.
I have said that we must endeavour to put our own house in order before we embark on an international scale. I hardly need say that during the period from 1929 to 1939 the gold standards and all the other devices they could think of failed dismally in this country. Why did not the gold standard system or scheme prove a success at that time? Why did we have to abandon the gold standard during the war? Simply because we knew that to tie ourselves to this mechanism or this scheme would not solve the problems of the nation. Now, in the peace-time period, no system which will tie Canadian currency and credit to any basis of gold will help Canada to distribute her goods and services, rehabilitate her returned men, and assist in putting this nation on its feet economically.
I will add only one other thought, I consider that all these international schemes are carefully and cleverly aimed at reducing the nower of the British commonwealth of nations. For centuries the British empire has been the bulwark of freedom and democracy, and we must not permit any scheme to be introduced. piece by piece, until we finally realize that we have surrendered our sovereignty and those liberties for which the British people have fought for more than a thousand years.
If this measure is as important as the minister says and as other hon. members who have supported it claim that it is, it should receive the fullest scrutiny and the most careful consideration; and I for one cannot see how we can examine the proposals as closely as we should, or discuss them as thoroughly as we should, in the short space of time remaining at our disposal. I fail to understand why the minister did not bring in this measure at the very beginning of the session. It is one of the most important measures. Why has it been postponed until practically the last week of this session? I do not wish to impute motives to the minister or his advisers, but I suppose it was expected that during the dying days of the session the measure could be rushed through this house

without much trouble and of course the government would not have to put up such a very strong fight.
Therefore, in closing, Mr. Speaker, I urge the minister, even at this time, to give the most careful consideration to this suggestion.
I do not believe he would lose much if he postponed the discussion of this issue for a time, or left it over to the next session, so that the people of the nation may be better informed upon it and hon. members have had ample opportunity to discuss it as thoroughly as they should.

Mr. PATRICK H. ASHBY (Edmonton East): Mr. Speaker, there seems to be some doubt in the minds of many members as to whether Bretton Woods is on or off the gold standard. I submit that Bretton Woods has set up a new gold standard. We are as much as told that we can either take it or lump it. Here it is on page 31:
Par value of the currency of each member shall be expressed in terms of gold as a common denominator or in terms of the United States dollar of the weight and fineness in effect on July 1, 1944.
There it is, as bold and as impudent as it could be. It may have had a little dirt washed over it, but it is the same old carat; it may have been increased to sixteen carats, but it is still there; it is the same old gold standard. I do not claim to be an expert oh gold. I personally put very little value on gold. Most certainly this metal has an increasingly minor role to play in the economics of most nations. What I am concerned with are results.
At page 205 of the Fortnightly Review for December, 1944, is an article written by one of the leading authorities on gold and finance. In fact, he was the co-editor of two Paris economic weeklies from 1935 up to the outbreak of the war and economic consultant to
various British and French firms in Paris, a graduate of Lausanne university, a doctor of social science, and he has contributed articles and political subjects to journals in Paris, London and New York. If he were not an authority this publication would not publish any statements from him. He said, at page 205 of the Fortnightly Review, under the heading, "The Role of Gold":
Bretton Woods set up a new gold standard. Any attempt to explain away the provisions of fund agreement article IV section 1 (a) on this point is condemned to failure. It may be better or worse than its pre-1914 or 1925 predecessors. That is open to argument. What is not open to argument is the fact that its reintroduction is in the overwhelming interest of the United States of America which, with a gold stock of $20,000 million dollars, is fundamentally concerned in preventing its demonetization.
It may be better or worse, but it is still a gold standard, and I feel sure that it is worse. When we speak of the United States of America we do not mean the people of the United States of America. What we mean.are the financial dictators called financial experts, with their vaults of gold, who control the lives of the people of that country and who hope to control the world. They are the supreme yet hidden power whose methods they are determined shall be upheld and maintained at all costs. This insane gold standard is wrong. It does not matter what system or standard we use; if the results are not what we want the wrong methods or the wrong standards are being used. The gold standard has never given and will never give us the results we desire. It always has and always will produce fear, poverty, wretchedness and insecurity, with ever-increasing debts and taxation, breeding crime and vice and ending up in periodic wars of ever-increasing violence. It is not the duty of the people we represent to adjust their lives and living conditions to a gold standard or to any other method or system whatsoever. It is our duty, sir, as representatives of the people to learn what results our people desire and want and then to instruct the experts whoim we have appointed to devise ways and means that will produce those results. The people must hold us, the members of this parliament, responsible for all sickness and for all deaths in Canada caused by a lack of any food, clothing or shelter. They should hold us responsible for all crimes committed for financial gain. They should hold us responsible for all conditions of poverty and suffering as long as the materials required are not available or .potentially available in Canada.
Likewise we must hold our appointed experts responsible, and it is our duty to our people to transmit to them the names of the
Bretton Woods Agreements

individuals who are responsible for the financial system and for even attempting again to introduce and fasten upon us another gold standard. It is the duty of this parliament to remove from office any expert who does not obey our instructions. We must not serve finance but serve our people, who have chosen us in good faith to represent their will. It is the duty of the experts first to obtain from this parliament instructions as to what the people want, and then make their plans accordingly.
In this Bretton Woods agreement these international financial dictators responsible to no one have, without any instructions from us, devised a certain system and standards, with full knowledge, we must admit, of what the results will be; they have introduced a new gold standard for a purpose, and the purpose or result they know must follow is not one, I can assure this house, that will create a happy, contented and prosperous nation of people. It is designed, I feel certain, to repeat in a more drastic form the conditions which the gold standard has always brought about.
I spent some time when a student at Oxford in studying .money and discovered that the whole system was based on fraud. Until we replace this system with an honest method, the results will always be disastrous. We must learn to distinguish between means and end. between methods and results. We do not want par value of currency expressed in terms of gold or old umbrellas. What we want is corned beef and cabbage. In other words, we want what we want when and where we want it.
In 1894 it was clearly stated by some of the world's keenest economists that the gold standard means inevitable war. But once war is brought upon us, gold is abandoned and money as required for destructive purposes is created in abundance. The gold standard means inevitable war. We know that. We have had several wars during the lifetime of many hon. members now present. Modern wars do not just happen. We are being ruled, not being served, by those who worship gold.
I wish the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) would not look so glum. Let us be cheerful about the matter. We have not lost yet. In fact, if this government only realized it, they stand to-day in a position which could be used and long remembered by humanity for many generations to come. In the hungry thirties I decided to go off the gold standard and to go on a standard that was backed, but not by worthless metal. I decided to go on a standard backed by real assets. I went

off the gold standard and on to the turkey standard. I believe in that old slogan, a chicken in every pot; but my slogan in the hungry thirties, when we could not sell our turkeys, was a turkey on every table.
What we want to-day is not counterfeit money, but genuine money, money backed by the real available assets created by the people. As I have said, I went off the gold standard and on to the turkey standard. That is true. In the hungry thirties I received bills as usual. At first it was just an ordinary bill, and I would set it to one side hoping I might be able to meet it the next month. When the next month came, a word was added to the bill, the word "please"; and then the next month still more words were added, "please remit". "Past due" would, appear on the bill the next month, and so on, until finally many of them gave up hope of ever being able to collect from a farmer who possessed untold wealth in the form of food which nobody could buy.
Consequently I started in to make some money myself. I know that the chartered banks had greater facilities than I had. They made beautiful bills, some of them highly coloured, and on each of them was the picture of the president or the vice-president. My bills had to be made of common ordinary paper, but I wanted mine to look fairly good too. Indeed I tried to embellish them. Now, whose picture should I put on my bills? Well, money is nothing but a joke, and the greatest joke in the funny papers was old Major Hoople, so that I cut out the picture of that notorious gentleman and pasted it on my bills, one of which I now hold in my hand. On the left-hand side is a picture of Major Hoople, the big joke, and on the other side is his wife Martha; for my money, if it amounted to anything, had to have some force and push behind it, and she was the one who was always pushing the major around. As it looked a little bare, I also stuck a tuberculosis seal on it.
Armed with about $75 of this money which I had made myself I went to town to pay my bills. I did have a little difficulty at first, but I explained that my bills were genuine money, the only genuine money in circulation, that my money represented real available assets. I explained to people that my bank would never have to close its doors, that I was not afraid of running my bank, because there were goods at any time available to all who wanted them in the form of turkeys, whereas a bank, if too many begin to collect their money, will close its doors since it has nothing back of its money, nothing whatsoever but pure unadulterated bunkum.

I feel somewhat under an obligation to say a few' words because I was a delegate from Canada to the conference at Bretton Woods. In view of that fact I considered that I should make a few comments on some of the speeches which have been made. First, in regard to our own experts who attended that conference, it is well known to the members who were there -their names are to be found in the final act of the united nations monetary and financial conference at page 6-that our experts were the equals of any there. I watched those experts in action, and I came to the conclusion that Canada had economists who were certainly able to hold their own in discussion with economists from any other part of the world. I feel that I would not be doing justice to our own outstanding economists who attended that conference if I did not say that.
Further they played a more vital part in the conference than those from many other

Bretton Woods Agreements

nations, because of Canada's position with reference to the United States of America and United Kingdom. When from time to time it appeared that there was some conflict between the United Kingdom viewpoint and the viewpoint of the United States, the Canadian delegation more than once performed the very great service of helping to reconcile the viewpoints of the two parties.
With regard to the suggestion that Great Britain has been clubbed into accepting Bretton Woods, I take it that that is based upon the idea that Great Britain did not agree to enter Bretton Woods until the loan of over four billion dollars was actually agreed to. It was well understood at the time of the conference that this international monetary fund could not possibly hope to function unless Great Britain was given a loan which would enable her to tide herself over the difficult period which it was known would follow the war. That was well understood by everybody there. Naturally, Great Britain could not possibly hope to carry out her obligations under Bretton Woods unless the interval after the end of the war was bridged by a loan which would enable her to get on her feet once more and begin to be able to pay for her necessary imports by exports. Therefore any suggestion that she was clubbed into submission, or anything of that sort, is not well founded.
There is this further thought; having watched Lord Keynes and his associates on the United Kingdom delegation in action, I can say in all sincerity that I do not think for a single minute that a man such as Lord Keynes has shown himself to be, one of the outstanding economists of the world, or his outstanding and able associates would agree to anything that would harm their own country and the British commonwealth of nations.
There is some suggestion that this is going to tie the nations of the world to gold. It was well understood in the British parliament before Lord Keynes came across to attend this conference, that Great Britain would not permit her currency being tied rigidly to gold. That was one of the reasons why the conference took longer than was originally expected. In other words, there had to be a formula whereby Great Britain would be able to have elasticity in her internal set-up, and should not be tied rigidly to gold.
When my hon. friends of the Social Credit party, for whom I have the greatest amount of friendship, suggest that, when a man like Keynes starts out from the United Kingdom pledging himself that he will not permit his country to be tied to gold at this conference, and when he says after he goes back that he has not, that he has carried out his promise,

he has not done so, that in spite of that we are tied to gold, then I submit that they are saying something which in their own minds they must find it very hard to believe.

The hon. member says that they will prove it. This is a most complicated agreement; it is a complicated mechanism, and for anybody in this house to take that mechanism and by citing a clause here and a clause there without citing the qualifying clauses and the escape clauses, and try to arouse fear on the part of the people who cannot possibly have a chance to study this in all its implications, he is not fulfilling the responsibility which I think we owe to those who sent us here to work for them.
From the best study which I was able to give this matter at the time I attended the conference and since I say that when Lord Keynes said that this agreement does not mean that we are tied to gold, in my humble opinion I believe he is telling the truth and nothing but the truth. There were people at the conference who were just as anxious that they should not be tied to gold as my hon. friends can possibly be. For example, the representatives from Australia and New Zealand were very much exercised about this matter. I refer to men like the Right Hon. Walter Nash, a man just as anxious about it as my hon. friends are, and who believes in their ideas to a certain extent, who watched from this viewpoint the working out of this agreement very carefully. I submit to my hon. friends, who often have spoken with approval of the opinion of the Right Hon. Walter Nash, that he would not have agreed to the Bretton Woods conference findings if he had not been satisfied that the freedom of action of New Zealand to build up a high level of employment within her own country was fully preserved even after they agreed to adhere to the Bretton Woods decision.
There is one other matter on which I feel I should say something. There has been some suggestion that in its attitude to the international monetary fund and the international bank for reconstruction and development the United States is motivated by some scheme of imperialism, of getting control of the rest of the world. In reply to that suggestion I would say that the conference was called by the late President Roosevelt, who sent to it as his representatives some of his best economists and closest friends. When the conflicting viewpoints were being discussed and it was proving difficult to reconcile them, one always felt the driving force of that great humanitarian President of the United States

Bretton Woods Agreements
behind the suggestion that the conference must not fail. Remember, the war was not yet won; Dumbarton Oaks had not yet occurred; we did not have the united nations organization set up. This was one of the first attempts to establish a scheme of cooperation among the nations of the world. We heard more than once that it was the wish of the President of the United States that the conference should succeed in its work in working out a basis of agreement in regard to setting up a clearing-house for the currencies of the world and also for the setting up of a bank which would help rebuild the war-torn world. To hon. members who suggest that in some way this is aimed at the British commonwealth I say, that in its darkest days the British commonwealth had no greater or more valuable friend than Mr. Roosevelt. When it is suggested that he would lend his great position, prestige and power to the drawing up of an agreement concerning this plan with some ulterior motive in view, some imperialistic motive, with the intention of destroying the British commonwealth, I say that suggestion comes with ill grace from anyone on the floor of this Canadian parliament representing a people who were touched to the heart with gratitude when in the darkest days of the war they heard that great president say that his great and powerful nation would not stand idly by and see us overrun and conquered by a foreign nation. I should like it made perfectly clear, in all fairness to the honoured memory of that great leader of mankind, that he could not possibly have had in mind any thought of dominating the rest of the world or of breaking up the British commonwealth when he arranged for this conference and urged those representing him there to reach an agreement.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me remind you that the way of mankind down through the ages has not been easy. It was not easy during the war that is just over. I have spoken to people who have seen what has happened in Europe, and they say the things that happened there are so terrible it is of no use trying to describe them, because the ordinary human mind cannot conceive of these things happening to fellow human beings. During the first great war those who wanted to escape the direct impact of war felt that all they had to do was remain neutral, and the war would not touch them. Well, some of the nations which adopted that policy during the first great war were among those who suffered most terribly in this war. And the people who suffered were the ordin-47696-1973
ary working people of the world. It is they who pay in large measure the price in human suffering and human misery.
To those who oppose this agreement I say that, like any international agreement, it cannot wholly satisfy every nation that adheres to it. The main thing is that mankind should come to international agreements in all phases of activity. If we learn to work together in the conduct of economic affairs, the settling of international disputes, the settling of disputes in regard to the use of raw materials, the setting of fair prices to primary producers the world over, the fixing of fair wages for all the workers of the world, the controlling of cartels and combines, and in regard to all the other things that require international action; if we achieve real success in dealing with them, we are well on the way to enduring peace. I suggest that it would be a most retrograde step, when forty-four nations have agreed on these proposals, for Canada, which depends perhaps more than any other country in the world on international trade, to be the one country questioning the motives of the power which originated this plan and which is making the greatest contribution to its success. I say that we owe it to the past and to the future to see that this step is taken, and to see that it is not the last step toward1 international cooperation in all fields of human endeavour. We must press forward along the way to ultimate world peace in all realms of human activity.

They have armed guards during the day to keep their enemies away- that is something which we do not have. They are behind walls of steel and concrete at night to keep their enemies away-and that is something we do not have. They have freedom of worship. In a well-run gaol the authorities will supply assistance by way of priest or rabbi or minister of the gospel to any man to help him to worship in his own way without molestation. But there is one thing which men in these well-run gaols do not have, and that is freedom of choice whether they will stay inside the gaol or go outside; and that is the reason why so many take their lives in their hands to break gaol and get out. They want that freedom; and all the other freedoms and security they have inside the gaol mean nothing to them without freedom of choice-real freedom. One other thing, Mr. Speaker, referring to experts. We have not made light of the experts, but we have pointed out that experts have differed greatly in opinion about Bretton Woods. They have differed so radically that it arouses in thinking men suspicion and a determination to go into this thing and find out what it is really made of. If there were

It is because of that fact that we question the finality of this expert opinion. We can agree that it is necessary to have expert opinion and we are glad to have it. But it is the responsibility of members of this house to find out for themselves. Experts can be wrong, and they have been wrong. I point out to my hon. friend what Winston Churchill confessed about what "experts" deluded him into doing in 1925. This measure requires the most careful study, because the results may be most disastrous, first to the debtor nations, and then ultimately to our own and other creditor nations. The very fact that authorities differ so widely not only in their interpretations of Bretton Woods but also in their conception of the whole thing, that some say it is related to the gold standard and others that it is not so related, that one group says it will solve our problems or resolve some of our national and international difficulties, and another group says it will not, but that it will aggravate them, should give us ample reason for pause. It ought to make us determined not to rush headlong into an agreement like Bretton Woods, without ample opportunity for full investigation and debate. There have been a good many things introduced into this house this session of far less importance than Bretton Woods, that have occupied far more time than it appears this will have, and it is high time that we changed that order of things and got down to important matters and gave them their proper place in the business of this house: That is why I think a vote of censure ought to be passed on this government for having failed to bring in this measure earlier and for having held it up until the dying days of this session and then trying to rush it through the house. That is not a thing they can be proud of.
There are literally hundreds of questions about Bretton Woodls that require full answers before anybody could possibly be in position to judge whether it is a good thing or not. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East that this measure should eventually go to the banking and commerce committee for full investigation. We would then have a chance to call in witnesses, examine them, get their views and straighten it out. I am prepared to go to the committee with my mind open. When I have heard what all the witnesses and members have to say I shall then be in position to judge whether it is a good thing or not. But to get those answers I say will take time, and plenty of time.
Some people, including the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Case) who spoke this afternoon, seem quite willing to commit Canada
Bretton Woods Agreements

to Bretton. Woods on the strength of the agreement of the experts from forty-four nations who met at Bretton Woods. I have already pointed) out that experts can be wrong. Many times in the past they have been wrong, and we are reaping to-day the results of the great mistakes that the so-called experts have made.
They can very well be wrong in this instance, more particularly because in approaching this question of opening world trade on a multilateral basis so that every nation may have access to a fair share of it, they have not approached the matter in any new sense at all. They have made a slight modification of the old approaches. It looks to me as though they have attempted to- put crutches under the tottering old economic system of scarcity. Any time that they attempt the same old approach we can expect the same old results. That is why I question very much the basis of this whole agreement.
It seems to me that the system which they are trying to bolster up by introducing this Bretton Woods arrangement has failed us so dismally in the past that the people of the world generally are seeking honestly for a new approach that is based on the real Christian principle, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." That is the only principle that we can ever depend upon to get us out of our difficulties.
The Minister of Finance ought to be anxious, and I pay him the compliment of thinking he is anxious, to give the members of this house full andl complete answers to the many questions that arise in our minds about Bretton Woods so that all of us who are the representatives of the people can feel reasonably sure that whatever we do in the end about Bretton Woods will be the- right thing, not only for Canada but also for the rest of the world. It i9 our responsibility to get the- answers to those questions. That is why we should) have had the resolution and the bill before us weeks ago. However, it is here now, and I hope that no one will attempt to discourage the fullest and freest possible discussion on the measure.
If the minister -can prove clearly in his re-outtals that Bretton Woods will assure to every nation access to a fair share of the world's trade; if he can show at the same time that Bretton Woods will facilitate payment by debtor nations for their imports without piling up against them burdens of unpayable debt and interest; if he can prove that Bretton Woods will contribute to the maintenance of world' peace and of peaceful prosperity, then I say to him that I will give him every support of which I am capable to get the measure through this house at the earliest possible time.

We in the house should examine Bretton Woods and all the arguments and the agreements in connection with it mainly from the point of view of the debtor nations, whose economic welfare these agreements are designed to promote in the first place. We should not worry ourselves too much about creditor nations and their welfare at this time. The creditor nations can be expected to get along quite well even if neither the international monetary fund nor the international bank for reconstruction and development ever come into being at all.

I wish to give my decision on the point of order raised this evening. I have considered the point of order raised by the Minister of Veterans Affairs with regard to the reading en bloc of the divorce bills reported to-night from the committee of the whole. I do not deny the minister the right to raise a point of order at the stage of the proceedings at which he raised it, but his point was that under our practice the question for third reading should have been put separately in each of these bills.
After mature consideration I have come to the conclusion that an objection to the question cannot be raised after the members have been called for a division; the objection should have been raised before that. It may be noted that the motion is that these bills be now read a third time. An affirmative vote will mean that they are read now. On the other hand, a negative vote would leave it open to any member to move that the third reading of one or more of these bills take place at a later date. Of course, such a procedure is seldom resorted to; nevertheless it is sound practice as shown in paragraph 756 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, which is a citation from Bourinot, pages 509-510, and reads as follows:
When the motion that the bill be now read a second time is negatived, the bill disappears from the order paper, but it is competent for a member immediately to move without notice: "That the said bill be read a second time on-next." On this motion being agreed to, the bill takes its place on the orders. The same practice obtains with respect to the bill, at any previous or succeeding stage.
So I will ask the Sergeant-at-Arms to call in the members.
